1.sense: The surah opens with a report, not a command: everything in the heavens and everything on the earth is already glorifying Allah. The two names that close the verse pair strength with wisdom, might that is never careless.

notes.t: This is one of five Medinan surahs that open with this same glorification, either as a completed verb (this surah and al-Hadid, al-Hashr) or a continuous one (al-Jumuʿa, at-Taghabun). Commentators group them as the Musabbihat.
The same opening sentence, word for word, begins al-Hadid and, with a small variation in verb tense, al-Hashr.

links.why: the identical opening formula, glorification already underway before any command follows it

2.sense: A direct question to the believers, no preamble. The complaint is not disbelief but a gap between claim and action, saying a thing without doing it. The next verse will name what Allah thinks of that gap before this one even finishes its point.

notes.t: The same accusation, that a group claims one thing and does another, is made of the Children of Israel earlier in the Qur'an, though there it is others' conduct they neglect rather than their own word.
Verse 3 repeats this verse's closing clause almost word for word, so the rebuke lands twice before the subject changes.

3.sense: The same failing named in verse 2 is now weighed. Kabura is the verb used for something too big to carry, and here the thing grown large is Allah's hatred of a claim unmatched by action. The sentence has no subject named for the hatred beyond the deed itself.

notes.t: Kabura maqtan is an exclamatory construction, a thing set down as enormous rather than argued into being so. The same pattern of verb, kaburat, marks a claim as monstrous in the story of those who said Allah had taken a son.
The construction kaburat kalimatan, a word grown great, is used the same way of a false claim spoken against Allah.

links.why: the same exclamatory grammar used to weigh a different false claim as enormous

4.sense: Against the gap between word and deed just condemned, this verse sets an image of matched claim and action: men fighting in His cause arranged in an unbroken line, each one holding his place like a stone set in a wall. The surah takes its name, As-Saff, from this single word.

notes.t: Marṣūṣ comes from raṣāṣ, lead: a wall whose stones are set with molten lead poured into the joints so no gap opens between them. The row is not just orderly, it is fused.
The same word ṣaffan describes Pharaoh's magicians told to come forward together in a single line, an unrelated formation that shares only the word.

links.why: the only other place the word ṣaffan, a row, is used of people standing together

5.sense: A historical case of the gap between word and deed: a people who knew Musa was Allah's messenger and harmed him anyway. When they turned their hearts away first, Allah let their hearts stay turned away. The verb for Allah's action, azāgha, is built on the same root the people's own turning used.

notes.t: Azāgha repeats the root of zāghū, they deviated, one verse earlier. Allah's action mirrors theirs rather than initiating against them; the turning is answered, not imposed.
Believers are told directly not to be like those who harmed Musa, after which Allah cleared him of what they said.

links.why: the direct command not to repeat what this people did to Musa

6.sense: A second case, later than Musa's. Isa confirms the Torah he was sent alongside and names a messenger still to come, called Ahmad. When that later proof does arrive, borne out in clear signs, the response is to call it sorcery rather than to weigh it.

notes.t: Ahmad is built from the same root as Muhammad, ḥ-m-d, praise; exegetes read it as an elative, the most praised, rather than only a proper name, so the description and the name overlap.
A hadith has the Prophet ﷺ list his own names, including Ahmad among them.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Jubayr ibn Mutʿim

notes.t: The Qur'an describes a covenant taken from every prophet to believe in and help a confirming messenger who would come after him.

links.why: the covenant every prophet took, to believe in and support the messenger confirming him

7.sense: The same rhetorical question that closed the Musa episode returns, but the label changes. There it was fāsiqīn, people who had stepped outside obedience; here it is ẓālimīn, people doing active wrong, fitted to those who fabricate a lie against Allah while being invited to submit to Him.

notes.t: The closing formula from verse 5 recurs almost verbatim, with the description of the people swapped to match the offense just named, deviation there, fabrication here.
The same rhetorical question, who does more wrong than one who invents a lie against Allah, appears elsewhere naming the denial of His signs as the parallel offense.

links.why: the same rhetorical question used against denying Allah's signs

8.sense: The opponents' effort is scaled down to a breath: mouths blowing at a light, as if speech alone could put it out. Allah's light is set against that breath as something already on its way to completion regardless of who resents it.

notes.t: This verse is repeated almost word for word later in the Qur'an, with Allah's refusal stated outright rather than left implied by the promise to perfect it.
The image sets a human mouth, the smallest instrument of breath, against light, which needs no defender; the mismatch of scale is the argument.

links.why: the same image restated with Allah's refusal to let the light go out made explicit

9.sense: States the scope of the mission just defended in the previous verse: guidance and true religion sent to prevail over every other religion, not to coexist quietly beside it. The dislike of those opposed to it is named and set aside in the same breath.

notes.t: This verse recurs three times in the Qur'an in nearly identical wording, each time closing with a different group named as resenting it, polytheists here, disbelievers and People of the Book elsewhere.
The same sentence closes with the disbelievers in one place and, joined to a description of the truthful witness, with the People of the Book in another.

links.why: the same verse restated with a different group named at its close
the same verse again, closing the sentence differently a third time

10.sense: A question posed as an offer, not a demand. Tijāra, trade, sets up the exchange the next two verses spell out in full: what is given and what is received. Nothing here yet says what the trade contains, only that it saves.

notes.t: The trade named here is spelled out as an actual purchase elsewhere, Allah buying the believers' lives and wealth in exchange for Paradise.
Tijāra frames belief and effort as an exchange with a return, not a cost with none.

links.why: the same trade stated as an explicit purchase, lives and wealth for Paradise

11.sense: The trade offered in the previous verse is named: belief, and striving with both wealth and self. The two are the only things a person has to give, and the verse closes by admitting that seeing this as better takes a kind of knowing.

notes.t: Wealth and self, amwāl and anfus, are a fixed pair in the Qur'an for what a person can spend and what a person can risk; neither alone is called the trade.

12.sense: The return on the trade: sins forgiven, entry into gardens with rivers running beneath them, and a dwelling named separately from the garden itself, as though the home is a gift on top of the land. The verse ends by naming this the great attainment, not a lesser one alongside something greater.

notes.t: Nearly the same promise, gardens with rivers beneath and pleasant dwellings in gardens of Eden, closing with the same phrase, the great attainment, is made to believing men and women together.
The dwelling is named apart from the garden, masākin ṭayyiba, as if a home were a separate gift laid inside the reward rather than assumed within it.

links.why: the same promise in almost the same words, closing with the identical phrase, the great attainment

13.sense: A second gift is added, one felt in this life rather than the next: help from Allah and a conquest close at hand. The verse ends on a command to announce this to the believers, turning the promise into something spoken aloud.

notes.t: Exegetes differ on which conquest this near fatḥ names, most reading it as Mecca, some leaving it general to any coming victory.
notes.src: commentators differ between the conquest of Mecca and a more general near victory

notes.t: A separate surah opens by announcing a conquest already given, described there as clear rather than merely near.

links.why: the conquest this verse calls near, announced elsewhere as already granted

14.sense: The surah closes by returning to Isa, this time asking his disciples who will help him toward Allah, and the disciples answering that they will. One group among the Israelites believed that answer and one did not, and Allah backed the believers against their enemy until they came out ahead. The command opening the verse asks this community for the same answer the disciples gave.

notes.t: The word anṣār, helpers, is the same title later given to the Medinan believers who supported the Prophet ﷺ; the surah's last word names its audience with the disciples' own answer.
The same exchange, Isa asking who his helpers to Allah will be and the disciples answering that they are, is told with Isa perceiving disbelief from his people just before it.

links.why: the fuller telling of the same exchange between Isa and the disciples
